article.title: Nithya Raman, Daryl Gates, and the History a Mayor Should Know
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Who Gets to Lead Los Angeles? Part One of a Four Part Series A friend recently asked me what I thought about the Los Angeles mayoral race. Before I could answer, she brought up something City Councilmember Nithya Raman had said during an October debate with Mayor Karen Bass. Raman had invoked former LAPD Chief Daryl Gates while criticizing the city's cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. For many Black Angelenos, hearing Gates's name associated with a supposed “gold standard” of police policy was deeply disturbing and for some it was triggering, I understand that reaction. I also believe the controversy has been used for political advantage. Both things can be true. It's possible that a candidate can make a historically insensitive remark that causes genuine pain, and then an opposing campaign can exploit that misstep to strengthen their electoral position. That's politics. But I am interested in something beyond whether Raman should have mentioned Gates (more on that later in this series). I want to know what we should reasonably expect someone seeking to become mayor of Los Angeles to understand about the people she hopes to serve. Daryl Gates Was Not Just Another Police Chief Gates served as chief of the Los Angeles Police Department from 1978 until 1992. His tenure is remembered for aggressive policing, racial profiling, battering rams, police sweeps, and an adversarial relationship with Black communities. Under Gates, Operation Hammer brought massive police deployments into predominantly Black and Latino neighborhoods. Thousands of residents, many of them young people, were swept into anti-gang enforcement operations, including individuals who had no gang affiliations. In 1991, the videotaped beating of Rodney King exposed LAPD brutality to a national audience. But the beating itself was hardly an isolated incident. For generations, Black Angelenos had known about and experienced police violence, and resentment over abusive policing had helped ignite earlier civil unrest, including the 1965 Watts uprising. What made the Rodney King beating different was not the brutality but the technology that allowed an ordinary citizen, George Holliday, to capture it on videotape and make the evidence available to the public. What Black communities had long described, often without being believed, could now be witnessed by millions. When four officers were acquitted on state charges the following year, the verdict helped ignite the 1992 Los Angeles uprising. These events were not abstractions to the people who lived through them. They shaped relationships between Black families and law enforcement, influenced how parents prepared their children for encounters with police, and left wounds that extended well beyond the individuals directly subjected to police violence. I know this from personal experience. In 1991, I was living in Lake View Terrace, the Los Angeles community where Rodney King would be brutally beaten by LAPD officers. My son was a Black teenager, coming of age and eager to enjoy the independence that teenagers naturally seek. He wanted to go out with his friends without adult supervision. Like so many Black parents, I had already given him “the talk”—the painful but necessary conversation about how to navigate an encounter with police, how to protect himself, and how to survive a situation in which simply being a young Black male could place him in danger. But having that conversation did little to ease my anxiety. I knew all too well that no amount of caution, respect, or compliance could guarantee his safety when confronted by a police officer willing to abuse the power of the state. One day, I shared my concerns with a white friend. Rather than understanding why I was frightened, she dismissed my fears, suggesting that I was taking things too far. I immediately regretted confiding in her. Something changed between us that day. I felt a distance that had not existed before. I had shared one of my deepest fears as a mother, and she had treated it as an overreaction. Less than a month later, the videotaped beating of Rodney King was broadcast across the country. It had happened less than a mile from my home. For me, the recording did not reveal a danger I had never imagined. It documented the very danger I had been trying to explain to my friend. That is one of the less frequently discussed consequences of racial inequality. It can create a schism even between people who consider themselves friends. When one person's lived experience is dismissed by another, the resulting injury is not simply disagreement. It is the realization that someone you trusted does not fully recognize the world you and your children must navigate. The Rodney King videotape allowed millions of Americans to witness police brutality that Black communities had described for generations. But for many Black parents, the question had never been whether such violence was a reality. The question was whether our children would survive an encounter with it. Mayor Bass was a community organizer during this period. She has spoken about her own experiences with LAPD surveillance and being labeled a terrorist by Gates. So when Raman described Los Angeles as a “gold standard” for non-cooperation with immigration enforcement during the Gates era, it is not difficult to understand why Bass and many other Black Angelenos reacted with anger. To be fair, Raman was referring to Special Order 40, a policy adopted in 1979 that limited LAPD officers' authority to initiate police action solely to determine someone's immigration status. She was not necessarily endorsing Gates's overall record. That distinction matters. But so does the historical significance of invoking his name. Raman subsequently apologized. An apology was appropriate. Whether the mistake should disqualify her from office is a separate question. The Difference Between Ignorance and Indifference I do not believe a person's failure to know a particular historical fact automatically demonstrates indifference. People have different interests, experiences, and educational backgrounds. Someone can be deeply interested in science and relatively uninterested in political history. Another person might spend decades studying literature without developing much interest in economics. We cannot reasonably expect everyone to know everything. But the standard changes when someone chooses a profession in which certain knowledge is essential. If Raman had become a veterinarian, I would have little reason to question whether she had developed a deep understanding of the history of Black Los Angeles. But she did not choose that profession. She studied Social Studies at Harvard and earned a master's degree in City Planning from MIT. Her professional work has involved housing, poverty, urban development, and public policy. She has served on the Los Angeles City Council since 2020. Now she is seeking to become the mayor of Los Angeles. Those choices create responsibilities. Urban planning is inseparable from the history of racial inequality. Redlining, restrictive covenants, discriminatory lending, exclusionary zoning, freeway construction, urban renewal, and unequal public investment shaped the geography of Los Angeles. We live with the consequences of that geography today. These were not simply mistakes made by individual property owners or prejudiced neighbors. They were often policies implemented or sanctioned by public institutions. Anyone whose professional life centers on urban planning should be prepared to explain how those decisions shaped the communities that exist today. And anyone seeking to become mayor of Los Angeles should understand the particular consequences of Los Angeles policies for Black Angelenos. What Education Should Produce I recently interviewed Robert Corsini, a white, Ivy League-educated city planning expert. Corsini spoke about the racial hierarchy embedded in American urban planning. His observations demonstrated an understanding of how technical seemingly racial neutral decisions about land use and development could reproduce racial inequality. I do not know whether he acquired that understanding through his formal education or through his own curiosity about civil rights and racial justice. But the conversation stayed with me. Why do some highly educated professionals recognize the racial hierarchy embedded in American institutions while others with comparable educational opportunities appear less attentive to it? Part of the answer may be personal curiosity. People naturally gravitate toward some subjects and not others. But that cannot be the entire answer when professional responsibility is involved. Curiosity is a personal inclination. Competence and diligence are professional obligations. A mayor need not personally experience every injustice that residents have endured. But a mayor should understand how those injustices shaped the city she has been elected to serve. What Raman Knows—and What Remains Unclear It would be unfair to suggest that Raman knows nothing about structural racism. She has publicly discussed discriminatory housing and zoning policies. Her work on housing and homelessness reflects an engagement with systemic inequality. Raman has also released a Black Agenda for Los Angeles addressing housing, homelessness, economic opportunity, and policing. But the document raises an important question beyond the merits of its proposals: Which Black community leaders and organizations participated in developing it, and how much influence did they have over its priorities? These distinctions matter. Recognizing structural racism is not the same as understanding the particular history and experiences of Black Angelenos. And developing policies intended to benefit a community is not necessarily the same as developing those policies in meaningful partnership with that community. None of this establishes that Raman is indifferent to Black Angelenos, nor would it be fair to draw that conclusion from a single debate remark. Nevertheless, I remain troubled. The most concerning possibility is not simply that Raman failed to appreciate the historical significance of Daryl Gates's name during a debate. It is that someone could advance through elite education, professional training, years of public policy work, and elected office without developing a sufficiently deep understanding of the particular history of Black Los Angeles—or without recognizing the importance of learning that history directly from the people who have lived it. I cannot establish that Raman has failed to acquire that knowledge. But her remark gives voters a legitimate reason to ask her to demonstrate it. How does she understand the relationship between policing and Black political life in Los Angeles? What does she know about the decline of the city's Black population? How does that history inform her proposals on housing, homelessness, economic development, and public safety? These are reasonable questions for someone seeking the city's highest elected office. A Standard for Every Candidate I do not believe Raman's mistake should automatically disqualify her. Nor should Black Angelenos be expected to dismiss their concerns because the candidate's intentions were different from the impact of her words. We should evaluate what she says, what she knows, what she has done, and what she proposes to do. The same standard must apply to Karen Bass. A candidate's lived experience can provide valuable insight, but it does not exempt that candidate from scrutiny of policies, performance, or results. The media has a responsibility here as well. Journalists should explain why Gates remains such a painful figure in Black Los Angeles, while also investigating the substance of Raman's criticism about immigration enforcement. Otherwise, a legitimate historical grievance risks becoming another campaign spectacle that leaves voters less informed. The question is not whether Raman is a good person or whether Bass benefits politically from the controversy. It is whether our expectations for political leadership are sufficiently demanding. What should we expect a candidate for mayor to understand about the history, experiences, and needs of the people she seeks to serve? That question belongs at the center of the election. And it leads to another, perhaps even more consequential question: What happened to the Black Los Angeles that helped build this city?
